title: Stamped "Blighted" Before the Bulldozers

place.label: The 1947 redevelopment study zone (Van Ness to Webster, Geary to McAllister), centred near Laguna and Eddy

hook: Years before a single Victorian fell, the city's own planners had written the Western Addition off, in language that singled out the colour of the people living there.
story: The paperwork came well before the bulldozers. In 1945 a study called Blight and Taxes, published by the San Francisco Planning and Housing Association, marked the Western Addition for urban renewal. It said the district "is not white. It is gray, brown, and an indeterminate shade of dirty black" [1]. The city's 1945 Master Plan praised the area's closeness to the financial district and its slopes for view apartments, then admitted that "only a relatively small proportion" of its "colored and foreign-born families" could be expected to live in whatever replaced their homes [2]. At the end of 1947 the City Planning Commission proposed a $52 million rebuilding of a 36-block zone enclosed by Van Ness, Webster, McAllister and Geary [3]. In 1948 the Fillmore, where 60 percent of residents were African American, was formally declared blighted [4]. Residents saw what was coming. In July 1948 a multiracial coalition met at the Buchanan Street YMCA, where Dr. Carlton B. Goodlett Jr., head of the local NAACP, warned that "scores of small businessmen would be wiped out by the plan" [2]. Demolition started eight years later.

title: Everything Came Down but the Schools

place.label: Raphael Weill (now Rosa Parks) Elementary School, 1501 O'Farrell Street

hook: When Western Addition A-1 cleared 108 acres, the plan said to demolish every building except a YMCA and two public schools. This school was one of them.
story: The Board of Supervisors approved the Western Addition A-1 redevelopment plan on May 28, 1956 [1]. Its 108 acres ran from Post Street south to Eddy and O'Farrell, and from Franklin west to Broderick. The plan called for demolishing every building except the Buchanan Street YMCA and two public schools: Raphael Weill Elementary, here at 1501 O'Farrell, and Benjamin Franklin (now Gateway High) on Scott Street [2]. Geary, a block north, was widened into an expressway [1]. Clearing the land displaced 1,350 households and 358 businesses, and a relocation office opened in the YMCA in February 1958 [1]. The area's population went from 6,112 before the project to 3,724 after it [2]. The Agency's final relocation report in 1963 claimed that "two out of three of the residents moved into standard housing" [1]. The longshoremen's union saw it differently, calling it "disgraceful that the Redevelopment Agency cannot even find two-thirds of the former residents of A-1" [3]. Most of the work was finished by March 1973 [1]. The school survived and became Rosa Parks Elementary, where the activist Mary Rogers later volunteered as a parent [4].

title: The Longshoremen's Answer: St. Francis Square

place.label: St. Francis Square Cooperative, Quickstep Lane (south of O'Farrell between Laguna and Buchanan)

hook: On land the bulldozers had emptied, a dockworkers' pension fund built a co-op where a three-bedroom share cost $610 and a family of any colour could buy in.
story: In 1960 the Redevelopment Agency set aside three blocks of cleared A-1 land for moderate-income garden apartments [1]. Lou Goldblatt, secretary-treasurer of the International Longshore and Warehouse Union (ILWU), wanted the union's growing pension fund put to work: "I thought there was no reason why that money shouldn't be used to build some low-cost housing" [1]. The ILWU-PMA trustees set up a Longshore Redevelopment Corporation. Architects Marquis & Stoller and landscape architect Lawrence Halprin designed 299 apartments in twelve three-story buildings arranged around shared courtyards, built in 1962–63 with a 3-1/8 percent federally subsidized mortgage [2]. A share cost $410 for a one-bedroom and $610 for a three-bedroom, and monthly payments ran from $84 to $140 [1]. The sales office advertised the Square as "open to all." In 1964 a new resident, Josephine Solomon, wrote to the Chronicle about "our marvelous, mixed-up collection of white, brown, and yellow children playing together" [3]. The co-op paid off its HUD mortgage in 2004 [2]. The city has not yet designated it a landmark, but SF Planning lists it as a proposed one [4].

title: The Queen of Fillmore Loses Her Crown

place.label: Site of the Blue Mirror, 935 Fillmore Street

hook: Redevelopment bulldozed her barbecue pit, closed her jazz club and had the sheriff carry her out of her tavern. Leola King fought the Agency for fifty years.
story: Leola King came to San Francisco in 1946 and opened Oklahoma King's, a barbecue pit at 1601 Geary that served buffalo, deer and quail. It stood inside A-1. King said she arrived one morning to find the building gone [1]. She was paid about $25,000 for the property and got nothing for the business she lost [2]. In 1953 she opened the Blue Mirror here at 935 Fillmore, a club with a circular bar and velvet festoons where Louis Armstrong and Dinah Washington performed [1][2]. The club was gone by the early 1960s. King said her liquor licence was taken after a set-up, and the Bay Guardian, which reviewed her records, reported that redevelopment reached the business and she was put out without compensation [1][2]. In 1964 she opened the Bird Cage Tavern at 1505 Fillmore. In 1974 the Agency bought that building for A-2, and the sheriff had to remove her [2]. She held two certificates of preference, and trying to redeem them turned into more than twenty years of legal fights [2]. By the late 1990s she had lost nearly everything, including her home at 711 Scott Street near Alamo Square [1]. She died in 2015, aged 96 [3].

title: A Congregation Rebuilds on Golden Gate

place.label: First A.M.E. Zion Church, 2159 Golden Gate Avenue

hook: Its old church on Geary stood inside A-1. The congregation rebuilt out west for $130,000, and its pastor later sat on the Redevelopment Commission.
story: From 1912 the A.M.E. Zion congregation worshipped at 1669 Geary Street, at Webster [1]. That corner lay inside what became the A-1 project area, bounded by Post, Franklin, Eddy and O'Farrell, and Broderick [1]. The old church was torn down in the late 1950s. In 1960 the congregation rebuilt here at 2159 Golden Gate Avenue, in a building designed by the architect Robert Batchelor that cost about $130,000 [1]. The Assessor's roll still gives 1960 as its year of construction [2]. Other Black churches were making similar moves. After the war, older congregations were either full or too far from where their members now lived, and their pastors moved them to the Western Addition. Third Baptist built at 1399 McAllister in 1952, and Bethel A.M.E. settled on Laguna Street [1]. By 1960 more than a third of San Francisco's African Americans lived in the Western Addition [1]. The church also kept a voice in how the district was rebuilt. Its pastor, Parree Porter, joined the Redevelopment Commission, taking the seat of Hannibal Williams, who resigned in 1978 after calling his fellow commissioners "white liberal zookeepers" [3].

title: Mary Rogers, WACO and the Bulldozers

place.label: Western Addition A-2 project area (centred near Fillmore and Turk)

hook: She had a ninth-grade education and twelve children. She lay down in front of bulldozers, and she helped take the federal government to court.
story: Mary Helen Rogers moved to San Francisco from Texas in 1965, just as the Redevelopment Agency was razing whole blocks of the Western Addition [1]. In March 1966 she and Hannibal Williams took the lead in organizing the Western Addition Community Organization, known as WACO. It brought together churches and tenants, including many residents of St. Francis Square [2]. Rogers had a ninth-grade education, but she became an expert in housing law, and on at least one occasion she lay down in front of the bulldozers [1]. On December 15, 1967, WACO sued the federal housing secretary to stop funding for A-2 [3]. HUD's own staff had found a shortfall of 689 units of relocation housing [3]. In December 1968 Judge Sweigert held that HUD's approval of the relocation plan was "completely arbitrary and without basis in fact" and blocked the Agency from forcibly displacing residents until it produced a plan for decent, safe and sanitary housing [3]. The injunction was lifted in March 1969, after HUD approved a revised plan [4]. Rogers kept fighting for forty years, until her death in 2006 [1].

title: The Promise Printed on a Certificate
hook: Displaced families were given a certificate promising they could come back. On this one block of Ellis Street, the city's list of affected addresses runs to 99 entries.
story: When the Agency took a house, it handed the head of household a certificate promising preference for housing built later. In 2008 an Agency spokesman admitted, "there wasn't a lot of housing built for a long time" [1]. A state law passed in 1969 made that priority a legal requirement, and the Agency's Certificate of Preference Program carried it out [2]. By 2023, the Public Press reported, city agencies had issued almost 7,000 certificates since the program began in 1967, and only 1,483 had ever been used [3]. Many of them, reporters found, were never honoured [3]. Today the city publishes the addresses of displaced households, with no names attached. The Western Addition A-2 list has 4,792 entries. The 1800 block of Ellis Street alone accounts for 99 of them, spread across 52 street numbers, and many list a flat, a floor or a basement [4]. Under a 2021 state law, descendants became eligible as well, and in January 2022 the city began issuing certificates to the children and grandchildren of people who lost their homes [3]. Investigators working with a city partner have tracked down eligible families as far away as Texas, the Carolinas and Georgia [3].

title: The Church That Built a Co-op

place.label: Bethel A.M.E. Church, 916 Laguna Street (corner of Golden Gate Avenue)

hook: As A-2 flattened the blocks around it, San Francisco's oldest Black congregation stayed put, built a new sanctuary, and sponsored 382 co-op homes next door.
story: Bethel A.M.E. traces its roots to a meeting house dedicated in 1852 as the pioneer Black congregation of San Francisco. By its own history, it moved to 916 Laguna Street on January 21, 1945 [1]. The church stood inside the part of A-2 that was cleared most completely. Between Ellis, Gough, Fulton and Webster, an area that had held about 2,500 Victorian-era houses was clear-cut entirely, and most of the replacement housing was two- and three-story townhouses built from the late 1960s into the early 1970s [2]. Bethel stayed and rebuilt. Under the Rev. J. Austell Hall it put up a new sanctuary and education building (1968–72 by the church's count, 1969–73 by the city's) and started a credit union in 1969 [1][2]. Hall also wanted housing, so the church sponsored Freedom West, which became the largest cooperative in the Western Addition [3]. It has 382 co-op units on about 11 acres bounded by Golden Gate, Gough, Fulton and Laguna, and the church stands at its corner [4]. Bethel went on to run Fellowship Manor for seniors, and later Prince Hall Apartments, Laurel Gardens and Thomas Paine Square [1]. A current plan, Freedom West 2.0, proposes to rebuild all 382 units [4].

title: Co-ops Built on the Square's Formula
hook: Once St. Francis Square showed that a pension fund could house working families, Black union leaders used the same formula to build co-ops in A-2.
story: In 1964, while A-2 was still being planned, the ILWU and its architects sent Mayor Shelley a proposal. Build first on vacant land, it said, and move no family until low- and moderate-income housing was ready for them in the Western Addition. Keep costs down with cheap land, low-interest loans, tax breaks and sponsors willing to forgo profit. "Basically," one co-op historian wrote, "it was the formula which made St. Francis Square possible" [1]. The union's plan also gave current residents first priority as new housing was finished, and the ILWU helped local African American groups build their own co-ops modeled on the Square [2]. Three of them are nearby: Loren Miller Homes here at 937 McAllister, Ammel Park at 656 Grove, and Martin Luther King–Marcus Garvey Square at 1680 Eddy [2]. Loren Miller Homes and Amel Park (the spelling varies between sources) were sponsored by the Labor Assembly for Community Action, a group led by Black ILWU leaders including Bill Chester and Leroy King [1]. The Assessor's roll dates the Loren Miller Homes building to 1972 [3]. In 1981 Leroy King became a commissioner of the Redevelopment Agency [4].

title: Twelve Victorians Roll West
hook: Over three stormy November weekends, a convoy of condemned Victorians crept a mile west through the Western Addition. Eight of them ended up on this narrow alley.
story: In late 1971 the new San Francisco Architectural Heritage group and the city's Landmarks Board picked out the best Victorians still standing in A-2 [1]. The Agency set aside 19 of them to sell for nominal sums, but 13 would have to be moved. Only two sold, and one was knocked down by mistake [1]. To buy time, Heritage entered minimum bids on the 12 that remained. The Agency got a $150,000 grant to cover moving costs, so a buyer needed only about $20,000 [1]. Over three weekends in November 1974 the houses moved west, most of them from the block where Opera Plaza now stands. Crews had to shift phone and power lines and Muni overhead wires along the way [1][2]. Eight of the houses ended up together along Beideman Place, the alley between Scott, Divisadero, Eddy and O'Farrell [1]. One of them, 736–738 Franklin, had been restored by 1977 and renumbered 33–35 Beideman Street [2]. The rescue was bittersweet. Some houses landed on lots where other Victorians had been demolished, and many low-income Black residents resented a rescue led, and bought into, mostly by white, upper-middle-class people [3]. About 2,500 other Victorians were demolished [3].

title: When Fillmore Street Went Quiet
hook: The "Harlem of the West" had clubs, barbershops and banks. After A-2, the stretch of Fillmore down to Turk stayed empty lots for decades.
story: A-2 was far bigger than A-1. It covered 60 blocks and 277 acres surrounding the first project, and the Board of Supervisors approved it on October 15, 1964 [1]. Work did not start until May 1966, because HUD would not pay for projects while Proposition 14, the state measure that barred anti-discrimination laws in housing, was in force [1]. Then the clearance came. Of 180 Black-owned businesses operating in A-2, only 48 were successfully relocated, and the other 132 went out of business [2]. Fillmore Street between Pine and Turk, famous in the 1950s as the "Harlem of the West," was left as barren lots for decades [2]. City officials later put the toll of Western Addition redevelopment at 883 businesses shut and 4,729 households forced out [3]. A co-op historian wrote that through the 1980s, the commercial life of lower Fillmore came to one Safeway and a few fast-food chains [4]. Willie Brown, looking back years later, said: "The black businesses, which had been viable, wonderful, and productive, were totally destroyed. The entertainment world for African Americans virtually ceased to exist in San Francisco" [2].
